title: With me?
description: Do you understand what I’m explaining?
details: “Are you with me?” means “Do you understand what I’m explaining?” “You with me?” is an informal version.

title: Flat out
description: Extremely busy.
details:
“Flat out” means extremely busy.

Example: “I’m flat out with work today.”

title: Rustle up
description: Prepare food quickly.
details:
“Rustle something up” means quickly prepare food.

Example: “I’ll rustle up a quick lunch.”

title: In a rush
description: Having little time; also “in a hurry.”
details:
“In a rush” and “in a hurry” mean having little time.

Example: “I need something easy to cook when I’m in a rush.”

title: Not a single…
description: Not even one example comes to mind.
details:
“I can’t think of a single…” means I cannot think of even one example.

Example: “I can’t think of a single reason.”

title: Beat the eggs
description: Mix yolks and whites with a fork or whisk.
details: “Beat the eggs” means mix the yolks and whites together quickly with a fork or whisk.

title: Omelette centre
description: The egg filling inside the tortilla roll.
details: In this recipe, “the omelette centre” means the egg filling inside the tortilla roll.

title: Tortilla
description: A thin, round flatbread. Say “tor-TEE-yuh.”
details:
A tortilla is a thin, round flatbread that can wrap around food.

Pronunciation: “tor-TEE-yuh.”

title: Filling
description: The food inside a wrap or sandwich.
details: “Filling” is the food inside a wrap or sandwich. Common fillings include chicken, beans, cheese, and vegetables.

title: Dried parsley
description: Dried herb flakes used to flavour food.
details: Dried parsley is a green herb dried into small flakes to flavour food. It keeps longer than fresh parsley.

title: Garlic granules
description: Small dried garlic pieces that add flavour.
details: Garlic granules are small pieces of dried garlic used to add flavour.

title: Kitchen staples
description: Basic ingredients you regularly keep at home.
details: “Store cupboard staples” are basic ingredients you regularly keep at home, such as rice, oil, and dried herbs.

title: Meaty texture
description: Feels like meat when you eat it.
details:
“Meaty texture” means something feels like meat when you eat it.

Example: “These mushrooms have a meaty texture.”

title: Flexible food
description: An ingredient you can use in many ways.
details:
“A flexible ingredient” can be used in many different ways.

Example: “Eggs are a flexible ingredient.”

title: Flavour boost
description: An immediate increase in flavour.
details:
“An instant flavour boost” means an immediate increase in flavour.

Example: “Dried herbs give the eggs an instant flavour boost.”

title: Presenter / host
description: The person leading a programme or video.
details:
“Presenter” or “host” describes the person leading a programme or video.

Example: “The presenter shows us how to make egg rolls.”

title: Pronouns
description: “She” can replace “the presenter.”
details: Pronouns are words such as “she” and “her.” “The presenter” is a noun phrase; “she” can replace it.

title: Present or past?
description: “She beats” summarises; “she beat” recounts.
details:
Video summaries often use present tense: “She beats three eggs.”

Past tense also works when recounting what you watched: “She beat three eggs.”

title: Salt and pepper
description: Say “pepper,” without an “s.”
details: “Salt and pepper” is the usual phrase for the seasonings. Use “pepper” without an “s” here.

title: New vocabulary
description: Say “some vocabulary” or “a few new words.”
details:
“Vocabulary” is usually uncountable when discussing words you learn.

Say “I learned a few new words” or “I learned some new vocabulary.”

title: Make a meal
description: A natural phrase for preparing a meal.
details:
“Make a meal” is the natural expression.

Example: “She shows us how to make a quick meal.”

title: What to call her?
description: Ask: “What should I call her?”
details: “What should I call her?” is a natural way to ask which name or role word to use for someone.

title: Common fillings
description: Ask: “What fillings do people usually use?”
details: “What fillings do people usually use?” is a natural way to ask what normally goes inside a tortilla.

title: Even though
description: It already shows contrast—leave out “but.”
details:
“Even though” already expresses contrast, so leave out “but.”

Example: “Even though I haven’t finished the video, I’m surprised by how easy the recipe looks.”

title: Summary recipe
description: Topic → two key details → optional reaction.
details:
Explain what the video is about, mention two important points, then give your opinion if you want to.

Framework: topic → two key details → optional reaction.

title: Keep it short
description: A short clip may need only 2–3 sentences.
details: A short clip only needs a short summary. Two or three sentences can be enough; you don’t need every ingredient or detail.
